newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Mahathir says Singapore leader should "make amends".
newsitem.headline: Mahathir says Singapore leader should "make amends".

text.p: Staging a rare protest against a neighbour, Malaysian youths on Thursday waved placards insulting Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew and demanding an apology for calling a Malaysian state "notorious".
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad declared that Lee, the former Singapore Prime Minister who now serves as Senior Minister, should make amends for his remarks about Johor state.
"The feeling among a lot of people in Malaysia is that some way or another he should make amends," Mahathir told reporters in Johor Baru, which lies just across a causway from Singapore.
In a deposition to a Singapore court on January 27, Lee said Johor was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
The Malaysian foreign ministry on Wednesday demanded an apology and a retraction of the remark.
A smiling Mahathir greeted more than 100 members of the youth wing of his United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) who hurled insults at Lee in a demonstration in Johor Baru.

They carried placards reading in English: "Kuan Yew stupid", "Mr. Lee you are senile", "Kuan Yew bloody idiot" "Kuan Yew must apologise". One placard in Malay read: "Kuan Yew is cursed. You are a pig. You've lost your mind".
The language was extraordinary in the usually circumspect ties among Southeast Asian neighbours.
In Kuala Lumpur, Human Resources Minister Lim Ah Lek on Thursday urged Malaysian workers in Singapore to return home, the national Bernama news agency reported.

"Malaysia would like them to work here rather than elsewhere because we are having (labour-short) problems, especially now when the Singapore government does not seem to value our good relationship," he said.
The opposition Democratic Action Party said it would move a parliamentary motion condemning Singapore if there was no public apology and withdrawal of the remarks.
Mahathir said the incident unmasked difficulties in ties between the two countries, which have had a simmering rivalry since Singapore left the Malaysian Federation in 1965.
"We have always had this problem," he said in reply to a question. "Although the public doesn't know very much, we've always had problems.
"We want to have friendly relations with Singapore. But to have friendly relations with Singapore requires considerable effort sometimes," he said.
Singapore had no immediate comment, and no official in Lee's office was available to talk about the uproar.

Singapore's stock market lost more than one percent on Thursday. While some said the market was taking its cue from the diplomatic flap, other market analysts said disappointing economic figures on Wednesday were a more important factor and questioned whether the row would have any the long-term impact.

Both Singapore and Malaysia are members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which ahs practically made it a creed to avoid criticising its neighbours. ASEAN also includes Indonesia, Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam and Brunei.

It was UMNO youth wing members, in fact, who forcibly shut down a conference on East Timor by non-governmental groups last November, saying it could harm ties with Indonesia, which annexed the former Portuguese colony in 1976.
But mistrust between Malaysia and Singapore is firmly rooted in history and culture, including the ethnic differences between largely Chinese Singapore and Malay-dominated Malaysia.

Last year the two countries had acrimonious exchanges when Lee raised the possibility of eventual reunification with Malaysia. Mahathir said then that Singapore was using his country as a "bogeyman" to scare voters ahead of Singapore's January elections.
